nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
June 8, 1990.  Thomas Czapla; NOAA SEA Division

FLELMR CODE: 5186

Common Name: Bay Squid
Scientific Name: Loliguncula brevis

Other Common Names: Thumbstall squid (14); least squid, brief squid (28); common gulf squid (180),  Atlantic brief squid.

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Mollusca
	Class: Cephalopoda
	Order: Teuthida
	Family: Loliginidae

nodes.title: Value
nodes.body:
Commercial: Squid sold through commercial fisherman are typically acquired as incidental catch from shrimp fishermen (745). The larger squid species (Loligo plei and L. peali) are the ones usually taken. Bay squid are sold in Texas supermarkets, but ordinarily not used as a consumer food (745).

Recreational: Bay squid are often used as bait in offshore fishing (28).

Ecological Role:  The bay squid is often a very abundant pelagic species in the estuarine zone and serves as a consumer of shrimp and fishes as well as prey for larger fishes.

nodes.title: Range
nodes.body:
Overall: Maryland to Florida, Gulf of Mexico, Caribbean, South America to Rio de la
Plata (14 317).

Within Study Area: During part of the year common off Texas coast but predominate on both sides of the Mississippi River delta, off the Florida panhandle and south west Florida below Tampa (745).

Movements and Migrations
Squid move out of bays to a few miles offshore during December and February to avoid the cooler temperatures. They move back to the bays in the spring when temperatures increase; this spring movement is also related to spawning and feeding (317).

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body: Bay Squid eggs are attached to submerged hard structures (J. Forsythe, per comm). Larvae, juveniles and adults are pelagic.

nodes.title: Habitat
nodes.body:
Type: Nektonic in shallow water of bays and inshore shelf waters. Distinguished among the cephalopods because it can withstand low salinity waters, down to 17 ppt and become common inhabitants of bays (317).

Physical/Chemical Characteristics: Abundance is correlated with lower salinity and higher temperature (317).

Temperature: Temperatures that are tolerated range from 11-33 C; possibly as low as
70 C. Low temperatures exclude squid from bays during winter the winter months, usually December to February (318). Bane et al. (28) reported temperature ranges for larval bay squid taken in nearshore waters off Louisiana as 11-25 C with the highest concentration occurring at 20-22 C. Benson (47) gives ranges of 5-34.9 C, preferring 13-16 C. He notes bay squid migration and abundance are regulated by temperature.

Salinity: Salinity ranges for squid are 20-37 ppt with the lower lethal limit being 17.5 ppt (317 297). Larval salinities taken from nearshore waters of Louisiana ranged 20-36 ppt with the highest concentrations occurring at 32-33 ppt (28). Benson (47) gives ranges of 5-35.5 ppt, preferring greater than 15 ppt. The lower salinities by Benson may have been taken at surface rather than bottom waters where squid were collected. Hixon (317) gives a lower lethal limit of 17.5 ppt.

nodes.title: Reproduction
nodes.body:
Repro Mode: Dioecious, transfer of sperm to female by means of a spermatophore.

Mating and Spawning: Juanico (370) reports bay squid perform head-to-mantle mating. A knob on the female mantle wall is formed for the attachment of spermatophores. Quality and duration of the spermatophore attachment is unknown (370). Spawning usually occurs March through December at depths of 2-18 m with peaks from April to July and a lesser peak from November to September. Eggs are deposited on sandy bottoms, some within estuaries (47).

Reproductive Capacity: In a single brood over 2000 eggs were produced. With multiple broods an estimated 1400-6350 can be produced by one female (317). Eggs are enclosed in a capsule; the number per single capsule is limited by size of individual eggs and the size of the spawning female`s nidamental apparatus (57).

Growth and Development
Egg: No information.

Larvae: No information.

Juvenile: Hixon (317) found growth among individuals to be highly variable with field averages of 8.6 and 7.9 mm/month for males and females respectively. There were no significant differences in growth rates between field and laboratory and sexes.

Adult: Males are sexually mature in about 6 months at a mantle length of about 40 mm; females at 8 months, about 70 mm mantle length (317). Slightly smaller sizes of maturity have been reported 32 mm ML males; 63 mm ML females (47).

Food and Feeding
Adults feed primarily on striped mullet juveniles, tidewater silversides, and Atlantic croaker in the upper regions of the water column. They also prefer white shrimp. ~f the prey move to the bottom without being detected they are not pursued. Juvenile bay squid preferred fish and shrimp equal to or smaller than their own size. Tidewater silversides, sheepshead minnows, and sailfin mollies were observed as natural foods (276 277 317). Seagrass has also been reported as a food item (47).

Ecological Interactions and Notes
Edible, but primarily used for bait. This species is sometimes used in neurosciences, because of the presence of a giant axon characteristic of the decapod molluscs.
